definition: Purine and pyrimidine nucleotides and their direct precursors.
Proteinogenic amino acids and the branchpoint intermediates of their families.
Neutral single sugars, including pentoses, hexoses and deoxyhexoses.
Nitrogen-bearing sugars such as N-acetylglucosamine and sialic acid.
Sugar acids such as glucuronate and galacturonate.
Glycan polymers and the decorations attached to them.
Proteins and the peptides released from them.
Builds a cellular building block the organism would otherwise have to acquire.
Converts an acquired substrate into central carbon metabolism.
Moves a substrate across the cell boundary.
Acts on dietary plant polysaccharides or the sugars released from them.
Acts on host-derived glycans or the sugars released from them.
Cleaves structural proteins of host or dietary animal tissue, typically as a colonisation or virulence capability rather than for carbon.
A polymer, glycan or protein; too large to cross a membrane.
A short glycan oligomer released by endo-acting cleavage.
A peptide or heterogeneous peptide mixture released by proteolytic cleavage of a protein.
A single sugar or sugar acid.
Any other boundary metabolite, including phosphorylated intermediates.
Enters the system from plant material, typically as diet.
Enters the system from animal tissue, as diet or as host tissue.
Produced by the host, typically as a secreted glycan such as mucin or as a structural protein of the extracellular matrix.
An intracellular metabolite of shared central metabolism.
An inorganic nutrient.
A building block a growing cell must obtain or synthesise.
Not itself a biomass building block.
An extracellular filamentous or fibrillar structure anchored in the cell envelope and built by a dedicated assembly machine.
A structure built within the cell envelope itself rather than projecting from it.
A machine whose curated architecture exists to translocate substrates across the envelope.
A sensor histidine kinase paired with a cognate response regulator.
A receptor-array signalling pathway with a coupled kinase, a diffusible response regulator and a receptor methylation adaptation cycle.
A system that distinguishes self from non-self DNA by modification and cleaves what is unmodified.
A system that recognises invading nucleic acid by sequence complementarity to stored spacers.
Aliphatic monocarboxylates of two to six carbons formed as fermentation end products. Formate is excluded by chain length and lactate by being a 2-hydroxy acid rather than a fatty acid.
An intermediate of shared central carbon metabolism, such as pyruvate, acetyl-CoA or a deoxyhexose cleavage product, rather than an acquired nutrient class.

Forms a fermentation end product as a terminal step of fermentation. The role names what the chemistry produces, not that the product is excreted, which gifter has no evidence layer for. Broadened from short-chain fatty acids when the organic acid layer added lactate, ethanol and acetoin.
Operates within shared central carbon metabolism rather than on an acquired substrate or an excreted product.
Carboxylic and hydroxy acids of central carbon metabolism that are not short-chain fatty acids, such as lactate, malate and citrate.
Uncharged fermentation end products such as ethanol and acetoin, formed to dispose of reducing equivalents without releasing an acid.
Enzyme cofactors and the vitamins that are their precursors. The chemistry is diverse; what the class names is that the product works as a cofactor rather than as a carbon or nitrogen source.

Produces a compound that other organisms, including the host, cannot synthesise and must acquire. The role states the nutritional relation; whether anything actually receives the vitamin is not something gifter can evidence.
Produced by other members of the microbial community and acquired from them, such as a salvaged vitamin precursor.

The GIFT is a segment of the oxidative citric acid cycle. The facet records the curated name of a cycle; whether a genome closes it is derived from the composition graph and the genome's own calls, never from this value.
The GIFT is a segment of the glyoxylate cycle. The facet records the curated name only; membership and whether a genome closes the cycle are derived from declared anchors and Boolean calls.

Benzenoid and heteroaromatic compounds and the branchpoint intermediates that supply them. Chorismate is included although it is not itself aromatic in the benzene sense: it is the cyclohexadiene the ring compounds are made from, and classifying it anywhere else would separate it from everything it produces. Proteinogenic aromatic amino acids stay in amino_acid, because what the class answers is which chemistry a capability is about, and theirs is amino acid supply. Ring-cleavage products such as 2-oxopent-4-enoate and 3-oxoadipyl-CoA are included as well: they exist only because a ring was opened, and classifying them elsewhere would split one degradation funnel across two classes.

Produces a compound that is not a building block of the cell and not a fermentation product, but acts outside the cell or on another organism, such as a siderophore precursor or a phytohormone. The role names what the chemistry produces; gifter has no evidence layer for secretion, for the receiving organism, or for any effect on it.

The capability's product is an aromatic compound whose ring is built by the shikimate pathway, whether the GIFT starts at chorismate, at an earlier shikimate intermediate or at an aromatic amino acid downstream of it. The facet records shared biosynthetic origin, which deliberately cuts across substrate_class: 4-aminobenzoate and menaquinone are cofactors, salicylate is a siderophore precursor and indole-3-acetate a phytohormone, and all four rings come out of the same pathway.
Inorganic nitrogen species used as a nitrogen source, such as nitrate, nitrite and ammonium.
Inorganic sulfur species used as a sulfur source, such as sulfate, sulfite and sulfide.
Urea and the cyclic and open-chain ureides of purine catabolism, such as urate, allantoin and allantoate.
Quaternary ammonium compounds and methylated amines, such as glycine betaine, L-carnitine, creatinine, sarcosine and methylamine.
Carbon-sulfonate compounds such as taurine and the sulfoacetaldehyde released from it.

Liberates nitrogen from an organic or inorganic substrate, or assimilates it, in a form the cell can incorporate into biomass. The role names what the chemistry does; gifter has no evidence layer for whether the nitrogen is actually incorporated.
Liberates or reduces sulfur from an organic or inorganic substrate into a form the cell can assimilate. The role does not claim incorporation into biomass.

Forms a compound that is neither a building block of the cell nor a fermentation product, and whose significance is to an organism other than the producer. The role names what the chemistry produces; gifter has no evidence layer for release, for the receiving organism, or for any effect on it.

Activates an aromatic ring for cleavage, cleaves one, or degrades a ring-cleavage product. The role names the chemical problem the capability solves; whether the substrate is a plant compound, a host or microbial catabolite, or an industrial pollutant is recorded on the anchor as resource_origin, not here.
Enters the system from industrial or agricultural human activity, whether or not the compound also occurs naturally.

A system whose curated function is the enzymatic conversion of a toxic chemical challenge into a less harmful chemical species. The class names the mechanism, not the outcome: a positive call does not claim that the organism tolerates or survives exposure. Efflux, sequestration and repair of the damage are excluded by the definition, because none of them converts the challenge chemical.
